messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh Tran had been working as an investigative journalist in his late thirties when he was detained during a reporting trip and tortured over several days by security forces who wanted names, sources, and admissions he could not safely give. He remembered the first interrogation room most clearly because of the sounds: a child crying somewhere down the hall, thin and persistent, and the scrape of a chair as someone leaned in close and said a name that sounded like one of his old contacts. Even now, when he hears children crying in a grocery store or on the sidewalk outside his apartment, or when a familiar name is spoken in conversation, his body reacts before he can think. He feels suddenly lightheaded, as if the room tilts, and he becomes jumpy to ordinary noises that would not bother most people. In those moments he pulls away from people, avoids seeing former colleagues he once socialised with, and tells himself he has to keep a low profile. He has also begun skipping meals or restricting food, saying it helps him feel less exposed and gives him some sense of control. What Minh has come to dread is not only the sound itself but the rush of what it brings back: the torture, the helplessness, and the way his mind reaches for explanations he cannot bear.

The memory does not come back to him in a clean sequence. When he tries to deliberately remember what happened, he finds it difficult to access the details, and what does surface feels strangely unreal, almost impossible to believe happened to him. There are stretches he cannot account for no matter how hard he tries. Yet the gaps do not bring relief. They leave him more on edge, scanning other people closely for signs that they might harm him, watching faces, hands, and posture with a vigilance that feels exhausting but necessary. He startles at a door banging shut or a pan dropping in the apartment below, and the jump itself sends him back into the same half-remembered terror. In that heightened state, he becomes convinced that other people can see what happened to him just by looking at him, as if the torture has marked his body in ways he cannot hide. He has begun to believe there is something wrong with him as a person, and that he acted in ways that go against who he is. Those thoughts deepen his fear and shame, and they make it harder to sit with anyone who knew him before, especially people from his old professional circle, so he keeps cancelling plans and staying home. The more he avoids, the less chance he has of finding reassurance, and the more the memories and bodily reactions feel like proof that he is damaged.

Minh’s days have narrowed around these reactions. He will leave the house for work assignments and feel his attention split between the story in front of him and the possibility of threat behind him. At his desk, if someone nearby laughs too suddenly or a child cries outside the newsroom, his shoulders tense and he loses the thread of what he is reading. Later he replays the event in his head, dwelling on how it could have been prevented, as if finding the correct decision might undo what was done to him. But the rumination only keeps the scene active, and when the torture memory comes into sharper focus he feels the same helpless anger, horror, guilt, and shame, which makes him even more certain that he is unsafe and fundamentally altered. In turn, that sense of danger makes him watch people even more closely, and the watching feeds the conviction that he can spot harm before it reaches him. The cycle has reached into his eating as well; after a day of being on guard, he often restricts food because eating feels too vulnerable, though by evening he is weaker and more dizzy, which he experiences as another bodily sign that something is wrong.

Over the months after his release and divorce, Minh’s avoidance has begun to affect his work and his relationships. He has turned down lunches with former colleagues, missed informal meetings, and spent long stretches alone in his apartment. He says it is easier that way, but the isolation leaves him with more time to replay the torture, more time to notice the unreliability of his memory, and more time to anticipate danger in ordinary sounds and faces. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent morning in which a child crying in the apartment hallway, followed by a neighbour calling out a name that reminded him of the interrogation, made him dizzy enough that he had to sit on the floor outside his own door. He is seeking help now because he fears that if this continues he will keep shrinking his life until there is nothing left of the person he was, and because, despite his shame, he still hopes he can learn to feel like himself again.
